text: Sequential consistency makes intuitive sense because it matches how we think about code execution: a neat, interleaving sequence of operations. But hardware gave up on that years ago. Insisting on seq_cst everywhere is essentially demanding that modern CPUs lobotomize themselves for our comfort.
context: Hardware architectures—x86, ARM, POWER—allow CPUs to reorder memory operations for performance, meaning a write visible to one core may not be visible to another in the order it occurred. The C++ memory model (C++11 onward) formalises this with `std::atomic` and six memory orderings, from `relaxed` (no ordering guarantees) through `acquire`/`release` (one-directional barriers) to `seq_cst` (total order). The live question is that seq_cst is the only ordering most programmers can reason about safely, yet it is the most expensive. The intellectual tension is between the formal correctness of the memory model specification and the practical difficulty of applying it: a single misplaced `relaxed` is sufficient for a data race that is silent under x86 and catastrophic under ARM.

The live question is that seq_cst is the only ordering most programmers can reason about safely, yet it is the most expensive. The intellectual tension is between the formal correctness of the memory model specification and the practical difficulty of applying it: a single misplaced `relaxed` is sufficient for a data race that is silent under x86 and catastrophic under ARM.

text: It’s important to recognize that std::atomic does not magically make complex operations thread-safe. It only guarantees atomicity for the specific type it wraps. You cannot wrap a massive struct in std::atomic and expect your multi-step algorithm to become concurrent.
